message.content:
Below is a concise, up‑to‑date summary (as of 2026) of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. These rights come from the Texas Property Code, local ordinances, and general landlord‑tenant law. If you need more detail on a particular issue, let me know and I can dive deeper. | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge a security deposit, but it cannot exceed **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit or **three months’ rent** for a furnished unit.
• The deposit must be held in a **separate, interest‑bearing account** (unless the landlord is a bank).
• Landlords must return the deposit within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Get a written receipt when you pay the deposit.
• Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report. | | **Habitability & Repairs** | • Landlords must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (Sections 24.001–24.004).
• You can withhold rent only if the landlord fails to make **necessary repairs** after being notified in writing. | • Document problems (photos, videos, written notices).
• Send a certified letter or email to the landlord. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For month‑to‑month leases: **30‑day written notice** to terminate.
• For fixed‑term leases: the lease ends automatically unless you give notice per the lease terms. | • Keep a copy of any notice you send. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must file a **Petition for Eviction** in the county court where the property is located.
• The court will schedule a hearing; you’ll receive a summons.
• Texas courts typically require a **just cause** (e.g., non‑payment, lease violation, or landlord’s own use). | • Respond promptly to the summons.
• Attend the hearing; bring evidence of your compliance. | | **Rent Increases** | • Landlords may raise rent at the end of a lease term or with **30‑day written notice** for month‑to‑month tenants. | • Review the lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Privacy & Entry** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or handicap. | • Report violations to the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR). | | **Lease Terms & Modifications** | • Any changes to the lease must be in writing and signed by both parties. | • Never sign a new lease without reading it fully. | | **Utilities & Services** | • Landlords must provide essential services (heat, hot water, electricity, plumbing). | • If utilities fail, notify the landlord immediately. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • The lease may restrict subletting; if allowed, it usually requires landlord approval. | • Obtain written permission before subletting. | | **Legal Remedies** | • If a landlord violates your rights, you can file a complaint with the local housing authority or TCHR, or sue in small claims court (up to $20,000). | • Keep all correspondence and receipts. | ### Quick Checklist Before Moving In 1. **Read the Lease** – Look for clauses on rent, deposits, maintenance, entry, and termination. 2. **Get a Move‑In Inspection** – Walk through the unit with the landlord and note any existing damage. 3. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts. 4. **Know Your Local Ordinances** – Some cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas) have additional tenant protections. ### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Property Code** | Full statutory text (online). | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR)** | Complaint filing for discrimination. | | **Local Housing Authorities** | Eviction assistance, mediation. | | **Texas Small Claims Court** | Filing for damages up to $20k. | | **Legal Aid Organizations** | Free or low‑cost legal help (e.g., Texas Legal Services Center). | --- #### Common Questions - **Can a landlord raise my rent during a lease?** Only at the lease’s end or with proper notice if the lease allows it. - **What if my landlord refuses to fix a major issue?** You can withhold rent *only* after giving written notice and waiting a reasonable period. - **Do I have to pay for repairs if the landlord is at fault?** No—if the landlord is responsible, they must cover repair costs. Feel free to ask about any specific scenario (e.g., “What if my landlord wants to increase my rent mid‑lease?” or “How do I handle a dispute over a security deposit?”).
